title: time-sampled population sequencing reveals the interplay of selection and genetic drift in experimental evolution of potato virus y
display_name: Time-Sampled Population Sequencing Reveals the Interplay of Selection and Genetic Drift in Experimental Evolution of Potato Virus Y

authorships.name: Santiago F. Elena
institutions: Instituto de Biología Molecular y Celular de Plantas

abstract: abstract rna viruses are one of the fastest-evolving biological entities. within their hosts, they exist as genetically diverse populations (i.e., viral mutant swarms), which are sculpted by different evolutionary mechanisms, such as mutation, natural selection, and genetic drift, and also the interactions between genetic variants within the mutant swarms. to elucidate the mechanisms that modulate the population diversity of an important plant-pathogenic virus, we performed evolution experiments with potato virus y (pvy) in potato genotypes that differ in their defense response against the virus. using deep sequencing of small rnas, we followed the temporal dynamics of standing and newly generated variations in the evolving viral lineages. a time-sampled approach allowed us to (i) reconstruct theoretical haplotypes in the starting population by using clustering of single nucleotide polymorphisms' trajectories and (ii) use quantitative population genetics approaches to estimate the contribution of selection and genetic drift, and their interplay, to the evolution of the virus. we detected imprints of strong selective sweeps and narrow genetic bottlenecks, followed by the shift in frequency of selected haplotypes. comparison of patterns of viral evolution in differently susceptible host genotypes indicated possible diversifying evolution of pvy in the less-susceptible host (efficient in the accumulation of salicylic acid). importance high diversity of within-host populations of rna viruses is an important aspect of their biology, since they represent a reservoir of genetic variants, which can enable quick adaptation of viruses to a changing environment. this study focuses on an important plant virus, potato virus y , and describes, at high resolution, temporal changes in the structure of viral populations within different potato genotypes. a novel and easy-to-implement computational approach was established to cluster single nucleotide polymorphisms into viral haplotypes from very short sequencing reads. during the experiment, a shift in the frequency of selected viral haplotypes was observed after a narrow genetic bottleneck, indicating an important role of the genetic drift in the evolution of the virus. on the other hand, a possible case of diversifying selection of the virus was observed in less susceptible host genotypes.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Evolutionary Biology > Molecular Evolution

title: recent emergence and spread of an arctic-related phylogenetic lineage of rabies virus in nepal
display_name: Recent Emergence and Spread of an Arctic-Related Phylogenetic Lineage of Rabies Virus in Nepal

authorships.name: Frank Wong
institutions: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation

authorships.name: Andrea Certoma
institutions: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation

authorships.name: Vittoria Stevens
institutions: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation

abstract: rabies is a zoonotic disease that is endemic in many parts of the developing world, especially in africa and asia. however its epidemiology remains largely unappreciated in much of these regions, such as in nepal, where limited information is available about the spatiotemporal dynamics of the main etiological agent, the rabies virus (rabv). in this study, we describe for the first time the phylogenetic diversity and evolution of rabv circulating in nepal, as well as their geographical relationships within the broader region. a total of 24 new isolates obtained from nepal and collected from 2003 to 2011 were full-length sequenced for both the nucleoprotein and the glycoprotein genes, and analysed using neighbour-joining and maximum-likelihood phylogenetic methods with representative viruses from all over the world, including new related rabv strains from neighbouring or more distant countries (afghanistan, greenland, iran, russia and usa). despite nepal's limited land surface and its particular geographical position within the indian subcontinent, our study revealed the presence of a surprising wide genetic diversity of rabv, with the co-existence of three different phylogenetic groups: an indian subcontinent clade and two different arctic-like sub-clades within the arctic-related clade. this observation suggests at least two independent episodes of rabies introduction from neighbouring countries. in addition, specific phylogenetic and temporal evolution analysis of viruses within the arctic-related clade has identified a new recently emerged rabv lineage we named as the arctic-like 3 (al-3) sub-clade that is already widely spread in nepal.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Evolutionary Biology > Molecular Evolution

title: the genealogical population dynamics of hiv-1 in a large transmission chain: bridging within and among host evolutionary rates
display_name: The Genealogical Population Dynamics of HIV-1 in a Large Transmission Chain: Bridging within and among Host Evolutionary Rates
abstract: transmission lies at the interface of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (hiv-1) evolution within and among hosts and separates distinct selective pressures that impose differences in both the mode of diversification and the tempo of evolution. in the absence of comprehensive direct comparative analyses of the evolutionary processes at different biological scales, our understanding of how fast within-host hiv-1 evolutionary rates translate to lower rates at the between host level remains incomplete. here, we address this by analyzing pol and env data from a large hiv-1 subtype c transmission chain for which both the timing and the direction is known for most transmission events. to this purpose, we develop a new transmission model in a bayesian genealogical inference framework and demonstrate how to constrain the viral evolutionary history to be compatible with the transmission history while simultaneously inferring the within-host evolutionary and population dynamics. we show that accommodating a transmission bottleneck affords the best fit our data, but the sparse within-host hiv-1 sampling prevents accurate quantification of the concomitant loss in genetic diversity. we draw inference under the transmission model to estimate hiv-1 evolutionary rates among epidemiologically-related patients and demonstrate that they lie in between fast intra-host rates and lower rates among epidemiologically unrelated individuals infected with hiv subtype c. using a new molecular clock approach, we quantify and find support for a lower evolutionary rate along branches that accommodate a transmission event or branches that represent the entire backbone of transmitted lineages in our transmission history. finally, we recover the rate differences at the different biological scales for both synonymous and non-synonymous substitution rates, which is only compatible with the 'store and retrieve' hypothesis positing that viruses stored early in latently infected cells preferentially transmit or establish new infections upon reactivation.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Evolutionary Biology > Molecular Evolution

title: the complete chloroplast genome sequence of a relict conifer glyptostrobus pensilis: comparative analysis and insights into dynamics of chloroplast genome rearrangement in cupressophytes and pinaceae
display_name: The Complete Chloroplast Genome Sequence of a Relict Conifer Glyptostrobus pensilis: Comparative Analysis and Insights into Dynamics of Chloroplast Genome Rearrangement in Cupressophytes and Pinaceae
abstract: glyptostrobus pensilis, belonging to the monotypic genus glyptostrobus (family: cupressaceae), is an ancient conifer that is naturally distributed in low-lying wet areas. here, we report the complete chloroplast (cp) genome sequence (132,239 bp) of g. pensilis. the g. pensilis cp genome is similar in gene content, organization and genome structure to the sequenced cp genomes from other cupressophytes, especially with respect to the loss of the inverted repeat region a (ira). through phylogenetic analysis, we demonstrated that the genus glyptostrobus is closely related to the genus cryptomeria, supporting previous findings based on physiological characteristics. since irs play an important role in stabilize cp genome and conifer cp genomes lost different ir regions after splitting in two clades (cupressophytes and pinaceae), we performed cp genome rearrangement analysis and found more extensive cp genome rearrangements among the species of cupressophytes relative to pinaceae. additional repeat analysis indicated that cupressophytes cp genomes contained less potential functional repeats, especially in cupressaceae, compared with pinaceae. these results suggested that dynamics of cp genome rearrangement in conifers differed since the two clades, pinaceae and cupressophytes, lost ir copies independently and developed different repeats to complement the residual irs. in addition, we identified 170 perfect simple sequence repeats that will be useful in future research focusing on the evolution of genetic diversity and conservation of genetic variation for this endangered species in the wild.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Evolutionary Biology > Molecular Evolution

title: debates the future of hydrological sciences: a (common) path forward? one water. one world. many climes. many souls
display_name: Debates—The future of hydrological sciences: A (common) path forward? One water. One world. Many climes. Many souls
abstract: all the world's a stage, and all the hydrologists merely actors. each plays many roles an accountant or statistician dealing with limited data; a physicist; an engineer; a chemist; a policy maker; a risk manager; and a diviner. seven roles or perhaps more. today, i am asked to play a speculator. it was a dark and stormy night, when our hero, columbus, set sail for the storied land of india. he found the bountiful americas. the natives were henceforth dubbed indians. an interesting story of prediction and validation if your prediction goes awry, then a correction by declaration is in order a bias correction in modern hydrologic lingo. i had learned in kindergarten that columbus's voyage disproved the hypothesis of the day that the earth was flat. it turns out that this is a myth perpetuated in the 19th century. the notion of a spherical earth was quite well accepted by 1490. the unknown at the time of columbus's voyage was the size of the earth, and the precise position of asia. the controversy was as to whether the distance to asia was as low as columbus estimated or much larger as the scholars of the day thought. the concern was whether the ships would run out of food and water before they reached asia. it turns out that columbus grossly miscalculated the distance to japan as 5000 km, when it was really 20,000 km. the ships arrived at the shores of the eastern caribbean, with a mutinous crew, at the edge of starvation. miraculously, columbus "discovered" the unknown americas almost precisely at the distance he had conjectured would be japan. today, india struggles to deal with the resource constraints of feeding and productively employing over a billion souls. the americas continue to be a haven for resources. perhaps, bravado can overcome poor prediction based on bad science, or sometimes you just have to be very lucky and set the course of history. with this example in mind, i offer an idiosyncratic reflection on the hydrologic sciences to establish context and then return to the task at hand to suggest a common path forward on matters related to water that transcend some of the traditional boundaries of hydrology. we live on the blue planet, unique in our solar system. it has abundant water in all its phases, and hence supports a myriad forms of life. hydrology is often described as the study of the occurrence, movement, and quality of water. it seems then, that hydrology has to be the most fundamental and exciting of the earth sciences. one can start with a basic question. what led to the formation and abundance of water on the earth? or another why and how the renewable supplies of water are distributed as they are on the planet? or what are the geochemical determinants of the chemical and biological constitution of water at any place of interest? or why is water essential for the origin and maintenance of life? or why in aqueous media, like-charged substances actually attract one another, when it is expected that they will repel each other? or how, landscapes are shaped by water, and in turn shape the course of water? or how variations in water fluxes constrain the development of patterns of drainage networks and vegetation, or patterns emerge at different scales in transport in porous media? many more such questions can be posed. all three phases of water play a fundamental role in the organization of the thermodynamic equilibrium, and hence of the climate dynamics of the planet. most major questions or uncertainties as to future climate projections for the 21st century are water related. they include: (a) the likely behavior of clouds, (b) the change in the transport of moisture and latent heat associated with this moisture through the atmosphere, (c) the form, intensity, and frequency of precipitation, (d) the extent and nature of sea ice, (e) the strength of the currents such as the gulf stream that transport heat from the tropics to the poles, (f) the degree of acidification and stratification of the major oceans, (g) the changes in regional vegetation, the associated evapotranspiration, and water balance, and (h) the changes in snow and ice cover and associated changes in planetary albedo. in turn, these uncertainties propagate to concerns as to the variable precipitation, runoff, recharge, and the chemical and biological quality of water that is available to humans and other forms of life at different places around the world. today, as many nations report a high level of water scarcity and/or pollution, there is broad concern about our water future given projected climate changes and population increase. an understanding and prediction of the state of water and its evolution across the planet is increasing in importance for science and for society. hydrology is a many faceted science. hydrologists often identify themselves as surface hydrologists, groundwater hydrologists, contaminant hydrologists, catchment hydrologists, urban hydrologists, hydrometeorologists, hydroclimatologists, hydropedologists, vadose zone hydrologists, social hydrologists, physical hydrologists, statistical hydrologists, engineering hydrologists, etc. while this speaks to the tremendous breadth and depth of the field, it also reflects a certain lack of synthesis toward hydrology as a planetary science. as one reflects on the questions raised in the previous two paragraphs, it appears that they are peripheral to most of what is taught in a hydrology curriculum or is in the forefront of research published in the established journals in the field. indeed, what we perceive as the hydrological sciences is largely focused on terrestrial hydrology, and within that on topics that are of primary interest from a functional perspective as to the organization and temporal movement of water and its constituents as they interact with the landscape (natural or as modified by humans). it may be fair to say that typically hydrologists attempt to model the spatio-temporal response of an open terrestrial system with external forcing that varies in space and time. prescribed time varying boundary and initial conditions are translated into a response of certain state variables, and the thrust is to identify how the attributes of a particular domain will determine such a response. this is the prediction problem, focused on the identification of a function that relates inputs and outputs, and there is usually a complementary forensic or inverse problem where the parameters of this function are to be estimated given some data. given a limited observation of the state of a system, the hydrologist seeks to either reconstruct attributes (e.g., past history) of the initial and boundary conditions or the key parameters of the model. in either case, at a conceptual level, the domain for the parameterization is implicitly fixed to a river basin or hillslope or urban scale, even if the analysis is performed at a global scale. this process is not so different from other physical and life sciences or engineering disciplines. the difference is that often, much of the temporal information content is determined directly from the exogenously specified climatic or human modification of the boundary conditions of the problem as one expects in an open dynamical system. consequently, the fundamental questions of water on the planet, examples of which were listed earlier, do not emerge as the centerpiece of hydrological inquiry. rather, we seem to focus on the response of a system to external input, and consider a limited set of feedbacks (e.g., land-atmosphere interactions research) to the driving climate and human systems. i realize that this statement may offend many hydrologists who work within an earth systems perspective and are interested in the nonlinear dynamics of the planetary system of which water is a key component. indeed, this culture exists, and i speak instead to the dominant threads in our field. hydrologic science considers the dynamics of the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy at any scale at which a model is constructed. there is much research on how one may try to close the balance in these equations given limited information as to the parameter that vary in space, and on the exogenous forcing of the system. clever schemes for parameter estimation and model calibration are devised, as are empirical models to predict time series, interpolate data, and estimate transfer functions. however, unlike some of the other earth sciences, there is less emphasis on phenomenological research aimed at discovering patterns or generating hypotheses related to the evolution of the system. this is not altogether surprising, given that in the usual representation much of the long term hydrologic dynamics is generated by the exogenous forcing. when we seek causal answers as to why there are patterns, trends, or oscillations in hydrologic time series, clustering of events, or extreme floods and droughts, inevitably one looks to forcings external to the typical hydrologic model. these can be a manifestation of the global climate or reflect changes in the watershed due to human activity, and the hydrologist tries to see how they are manifest in some local system. consider the typical efforts today to project hydrological conditions in the future. general circulation models of the ocean-atmosphere dynamics provide scenarios that are "downscaled" for use with hydrologic models to generate passive responses to these climate forcings. exploration of the possible feedbacks of the land surface into planetary fluxes and future states become the domain of the climate scientist. with this example, i do not intend to deride hydrologists, or to suggest that they need to become climate scientists to be useful. rather, i suggest that the hydrologist who tries to understand the long-term dynamics of water will necessarily operate at the larger scales that synthesize across climate and other factors, and may hence be better able to understand and predict the dynamics of the system of interest. the current era is being called the age of the anthropocene a time when planetary water, land, and air are being changed substantially by human activity. water has always shaped human habitation, and in turn, humans have played a key role in shaping the residence time, quality, and course of water. engineering habitats and water courses have been the fundamental ingredients of human settlement, navigation, migration, and trade for centuries. it is the rate and scale of these changes and the associated feedbacks on human and hydrologic systems that is of recent interest. in this spirit, in the beginning of the 21st century, a few of us (jose salas, jery stedinger, richard vogel, and i) coined the term hydromorphology to describe the "structure and evolution of hydrologic systems at the scale of years to centuries." by analogy to geomorphology, hydromorphology would focus on the long-term evolution of hydrologic systems from river basin to planetary scales, and encompass the full range of hydrologic processes across the planet. to give a flavor of the thinking, some broad questions that were articulated by the group included: how has water influenced the history of man and life on earth? how has man determined the history, distribution, and pathways of water? how have climate variations and change determined water and life at different scales, places, and times? how has water constrained and determined climate? how will the physical and chemical attributes of water, climate, engineered systems, landscapes, and human use of water coevolve in the future? at an abstract level, in addition to looking at the long-term evolution of the boundaries of the usual hydrologic system description, the idea was to start looking at a global water system in such a way that the human and physical system interactions are endogenous to the conceptual model of hydrologic evolution. this would lead to a more closed system with the forcing being primarily the external radiation input to the planet, and the interaction between the earth system processes and human dynamics focused on water as the central medium of interest. this would place existing hydrologic modeling paradigms in the role of defining structural relationships or transfer functions between the traditional forcings of hydrologic models and their outputs, and hydromorphology as the paradigm that allows systems level thinking about the potentially interacting earth systems that prescribed the boundary conditions of the traditional hydrologic models. speculation as to feedbacks across these earth systems that could lead to interesting structure in space and time could then follow. empirical investigations in this area are limited by data, but one could still generate hypotheses and explore their implications. hydrologic models may then be described through dynamic transfer functions with parameters vary across time and space in response to interactions that are local and global across natural and human systems. for instance, one could hypothesize that extreme floods or droughts in a region due to a recurrent climate regime that persists as wet or dry for years or decades, may depending on its recent history and oscillatory phase, stimulate investment in flood control and/or water storage structures in a region, which would then lead to subsequent modifications in regional hydrologic fluxes, and land use (e.g., diversions for irrigation of crops) which could in turn modify the regional land-atmosphere interactions and change the frequency and/or intensity of precipitation in the same region or at larger scales. such a process would reflect interactions between local, regional, and planetary scales of activity, and diagnosing, understanding, and predicting the impacts and consequences of such interactions at all these scales would be of interest. a hydromorphological perspective on water would thus bring together a scientific framework that establishes water as the important vehicle for understanding critical planetary science questions that link climate (ocean and atmosphere dynamics), ecology, geomorphology, and human dynamics. in summary, i laud the many accomplishments of hydrology as a terrestrial science dedicated to the understanding and prediction of the functioning of water systems at many scales up to the river basin, and welcome an era where we may embrace the functioning of our blue planet as a system defined by water through all its media and scales, with an engaging opportunity to understand the very march of past and future human civilizations. is there likely to be a unified theory across such an inquiry? does there need to be? in addition to individual curiosity and intrinsic search for knowledge, science appears to move forward in response to themes that are deemed important given some scientific, institutional, or social mandate. the themes of hydrologic change, global hydrology, and social hydrology are being articulated as timely and important. climate change and its potential impacts continue to be an overarching concern, with interest in prediction, mitigation, and adaptation. the projected global population growth, and its resource needs is another clear concern. the rapidly degrading state of the surface and groundwater stores in many places provides a focal point. collectively, these themes and concerns point to a time when water issues appear to be poised to define a critical and urgent research agenda that is not yet as visible on the global stage as it needs to be, in part due to the local nature of the science and the institutional concerns, and in part due to the diversity of seemingly independent issues related to water, each of which has importance. water is a primary planetary sustainability concern and it behooves us to shape the discussion from that perspective. a question that is often voiced in academic and governance forums is: "will we be able to feed the 9 billion people we expect on the planet by 2050?" this clear question and the agenda that surrounds it provides a focal point for investigations that range from the routine to deep scientific inquiry and technology development. even though "food" means many things, there is a global community that is organized around understanding and addressing this question from the perspective of population demographics, physical, and economic productivity, nutrition, population migration, distribution inequities, climate change and its implications for the changes in geographic suitability of crops, genetic and abstract: chronic infection with hepatitis b virus (hbv) is a major cause of liver disease and cancer in humans. mammalian hbv-like viruses are also found in nonhuman primates, rodents, and bats. as for most viruses, hbv requires a successful interaction with a host receptor for replication. cellular receptors are thus key determinants of host susceptibility as well as specificity. one hallmark of pathogenic virus-host relationships is the reciprocal evolution of host receptor and viral envelope proteins, as a result of their antagonistic interaction over time. the dynamics of these so-called evolutionary arms races can leave signatures of adaptive selection, which in turn reveal the evolutionary history of the virus-host interaction as well as viral pathogenicity and the genetic determinants of species specificity. here, we show how hbv-like viruses have shaped the evolutionary history of their mammalian host receptor, as a result of their ancient pathogenicity, and decipher the genetic determinants of cross-species transmissions.

title: host genotype and genetic diversity shape the evolution of a novel bacterial infection
display_name: Host genotype and genetic diversity shape the evolution of a novel bacterial infection
abstract: abstract pathogens continue to emerge from increased contact with novel host species. whilst these hosts can represent distinct environments for pathogens, the impacts of host genetic background on how a pathogen evolves post-emergence are unclear. in a novel interaction, we experimentally evolved a pathogen (staphylococcus aureus) in populations of wild nematodes (caenorhabditis elegans) to test whether host genotype and genetic diversity affect pathogen evolution. after ten rounds of selection, we found that pathogen virulence evolved to vary across host genotypes, with differences in host metal ion acquisition detected as a possible driver of increased host exploitation. diverse host populations selected for the highest levels of pathogen virulence, but infectivity was constrained, unlike in host monocultures. we hypothesise that population heterogeneity might pool together individuals that contribute disproportionately to the spread of infection or to enhanced virulence. the genomes of evolved populations were sequenced, and it was revealed that pathogens selected in distantly-related host genotypes diverged more than those in closely-related host genotypes. s. aureus nevertheless maintained a broad host range. our study provides unique empirical insight into the evolutionary dynamics that could occur in other novel infections of wildlife and humans.
